title: Latino optimism about intergenerational progress coexists with a cultural narrative that the American Dream is harder to reach
source_unit: Pew Research Center, Latinos Are Split on Whether the American Dream Is Achievable
geography: United States; Latino adults, with comparisons by nativity and generation

observations.period: October 6-16, 2025 survey; American Dream attainability among U.S. Latinos

denominator.unit: U.S. Latino adults in Pew National Survey of Latinos

achieved_dream.unit: per cent saying they have achieved the American dream

on_way.unit: per cent saying they are on their way to achieving the American dream

out_of_reach.unit: per cent saying the American dream is out of reach

dream_nonexistent.unit: per cent saying the American dream does not exist

harder_than_parents.value: Among Latinos who believe the American dream exists, respondents are more likely to say it has become harder rather than easier to achieve than it was for their parents.

observations.method: Nationally representative bilingual survey conducted online and by live telephone interview, recruited through address-based sampling and weighted to U.S. adult population benchmarks.
observations.uncertainty: The report notes that the 2016 and 2025 survey modes differ, so long-term comparisons are not directly equivalent; attainability is a perception and does not measure actual mobility or household wealth.
observations.subgroup: U.S. Latino adults, including immigrants, U.S.-born adults and respondents who say the dream is achieved, attainable, out of reach or nonexistent.
observations.counterinterpretation: A divided symbolic judgment can coexist with practical improvement; saying the dream is out of reach may express structural diagnosis rather than personal immobility.

observations.period: October 2025 survey; intergenerational living-standard outlook and nativity differences

denominator.unit: U.S. Latino adults in Pew National Survey of Latinos

own_standard_better.unit: per cent saying their standard of living is better than their parents’ at the same age

children_standard_better.unit: per cent saying their children’s standard of living will be better than their own

immigrant_own_progress.unit: per cent of Latino immigrants saying their standard of living is better than their parents’

us_born_own_progress.unit: per cent of U.S.-born Latinos saying their standard of living is better than their parents’

immigrant_children_progress.unit: per cent of Latino immigrants expecting children’s standard of living to be better

us_born_children_progress.unit: per cent of U.S.-born Latinos expecting children’s standard of living to be better

observations.method: Weighted survey comparison of retrospective and prospective standard-of-living assessments by nativity and U.S.-born generation.
observations.uncertainty: These are perceived and expected living standards, not longitudinal income, wealth, housing or consumption records; nativity differences may reflect age, selection, time in the U.S. and other composition effects.
observations.subgroup: Latino immigrants, U.S.-born Latinos, second-generation and third-or-higher-generation adults, and their children’s expected futures.
observations.counterinterpretation: Immigrant optimism may reflect migration selection or reference-point effects; optimism about children does not guarantee belief that institutions will deliver mobility.

observations.period: October 2025 survey; cultural meaning of the American Dream

denominator.unit: U.S. Latino adults; open-ended response coding in Pew National Survey of Latinos

economic_meaning.unit: approximately per cent tying the American dream to financial or economic factors; the report separately identifies 36% financial security, 31% economic opportunity and 14% homeownership

good_life_family_community.unit: approximately per cent describing a good life for themselves, family or community

freedom.unit: per cent mentioning freedom or being free

equal_treatment_acceptance.unit: per cent mentioning equal treatment, acceptance or freedom from discrimination

immigrant_economic_frame.unit: per cent of Latino immigrants mentioning finances, economic opportunity or homeownership, versus 55% of U.S.-born Latinos

observations.method: Open-ended survey question asking respondents in their own words what the American Dream means; responses were AI-assisted initially and reviewed/categorized into overlapping themes.
observations.uncertainty: Open-ended coding involves interpretive categories and responses can receive multiple codes; thematic prevalence does not measure the relative importance of each value in actual decisions.
observations.subgroup: Latino adults by nativity, language, national-origin background and meanings involving money, family, community, freedom, safety and equal treatment.
observations.counterinterpretation: Economic security and homeownership may be symbolic shorthand for autonomy, safety and family care rather than purely consumer aspiration; cultural meanings should not be reduced to market demand.

observations.period: October 2025 survey; perceived pathways to mobility and attribution of success

denominator.unit: U.S. Latino adults who believe the American dream exists, for pathway questions

hard_work_motivation.unit: per cent saying hard work and motivation are major factors in achieving the American dream

right_opportunities.unit: per cent saying access to the right opportunities is a major factor

luck_chance.unit: per cent saying luck and chance are major factors

luck_among_out_of_reach.unit: per cent among those saying the dream is out of reach who view luck and chance as major factors, versus 25% among those who achieved it or are on the way

agency_structure_tension.value: Belief in individual effort remains widespread, but perceived inaccessibility is associated with greater recognition of chance and structural constraint.

observations.method: Survey comparison of pathway beliefs by perceived position relative to the American Dream.
observations.uncertainty: Pathway beliefs are not causal explanations of mobility; the cross-sectional design cannot determine whether experiences shape beliefs or beliefs shape interpretation of experience.
observations.subgroup: Latinos who say the dream is achieved, attainable, out of reach or nonexistent, with attention to hard work, opportunity and luck.
observations.counterinterpretation: Belief in effort and opportunity can be complementary rather than contradictory; respondents may use luck to describe unequal starting conditions without rejecting agency.

related_sources.claim: Official Pew report landing page with survey scope, key findings and report materials.
Pew methodology page for sampling, weighting, bilingual fieldwork and open-ended coding.

boundary: This record adds a cultural-economic mobility layer: the American Dream is simultaneously a narrative of financial security, opportunity, homeownership, family and community life, freedom and equal treatment; Latino optimism about intergenerational progress coexists with a sense that attainment is harder and structurally constrained. It is nationally representative survey and open-ended coding evidence, not household income or wealth data, longitudinal mobility, causal consumer behavior, or proof of actual future living standards.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Pew report PDF, report pages on meanings and nativity, and methodology were reviewed for survey fieldwork, sample, attainability, intergenerational outlook, open-ended cultural meanings, pathway beliefs and sampling boundaries.
